title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Using Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation, two deterministic validators combined with a logical-OR scoring rule, and a matched sample of N = 300 intents (150 benign + 150 programmatic adversarial variants), we compared single-pass LLM generation (baseline) to an LLM+verifier GVR pipeline implemented under a frozen protocol (preregistration cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1). The adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics: one initial LLM candidate was generated per paired intent and the same candidate was replayed to both arms. The run completed all planned episodes with model_calls_used = 300 (shared candidate). Confirmatory outcome: baseline_success_count = 300 and guarded_success_count = 300 (contingency n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0); validators never reported forbidden reachability and the repair step was never invoked. Paired risk-difference = 0.0, McNemar two-sided p = 1.0, 95% bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Observing 0/300 violations gives a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994 on an undetected baseline violation rate. Because the repair path was not exercised, this study quantifies that inserting a verifier does not change observed compliance when baseline generation already satisfies the safety predicate under the chosen contract; it does not provide evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue genuine violations. We archive the preregistration, deterministic execution accounting, per-episode validator traces, and analysis artifacts to support reproducibility and to guide follow-up stress tests designed to exercise the repair path.

sections.introduction: Intent-driven configuration generation with large language models (LLMs) is an attractive automation path for NetOps, but operators rightly worry that automatically produced configurations can enlarge attack surface, violate access-control policies, or otherwise introduce security-relevant regressions. Prior systems and reviews therefore recommend constrained generation, execution oracles, and iterative generate–verify–repair (GVR) loops as operational mitigations. However, rigorous, preregistered confirmatory evidence that a verifier placed in a GVR loop meaningfully reduces forbidden-reachability misconfigurations under adversarial inputs is scarce. We set out to answer a narrowly defined operational question under a fully preregistered, deterministic contract: Does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of forbidden-reachability misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline? To make a clean confirmatory claim we fixed the pairing design, generation semantics, verifier set, and emulation environment in advance and archived all execution and analysis artifacts.
sections.related_work: Three threads of prior work informed our design. First, GVR and execution-guided repair architectures have demonstrated sizeable correctness gains on code and IaC benchmarks when verifiers provide targeted diagnostic feedback and repair strategies exploit that signal; reported gains vary strongly with verifier power and repair policy. Second, surveys and NetOps system research document recurring LLM failure modes—hallucination, domain mismatch, and overconfidence—and uniformly recommend validators or human oversight for safety-sensitive automation. Third, emulation and testbed studies show execution-based validation is feasible for research evaluation but emphasize external-validity gaps to production devices and live traffic. Existing work rarely combines a preregistered paired evaluation, deterministic validators, and archived per-episode verifier traces aimed specifically at security-relevant reachability predicates. Our study fills that niche by fixing generation semantics, trading provider-call budget for deterministic accounting, and archiving deterministic artifacts to permit exact auditing and targeted stress testing.
sections.methodology:
Design and estimand: The preregistration specified a paired binary design with N = 300 matched intents (150 benign seeds plus 150 programmatic adversarial variants). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute difference in the proportion of intents yielding forbidden reachability). The prespecified test was an exact McNemar two-sided test (α = 0.05); confidence intervals were to be obtained by a bootstrap-percentile method. Sensitivity checks treating technical failures as violations were prespecified.

Generation contract and adapter semantics: To limit hosted-model calls under the execution contract we used shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each paired intent a single LLM candidate was generated and the same candidate replayed to both arms. This design consumed model_calls_used = 300 for 300 pairs rather than two independent draws per pair (which would have consumed up to 600 calls). By construction the baseline arm is a replay of the same candidate rather than an independent draw; this reduces between-arm sampling variance and therefore reduces the probability of observing discordant answers across a pair. That choice was preregistered because the study prioritized deterministic, auditable accounting over maximizing sensitivity to repair efficacy.

Intervention arms and repair policy: Baseline = replay of the shared initial candidate. Guarded = the same shared initial candidate validated by two deterministic validators; if any validator reported forbidden reachability the preregistered repair policy allowed up to one repair LLM call (maximum one repair per pair). Repair attempts were only permitted when a validator-detected forbidden-reachability predicate occurred.

Validators, scoring rule, and determinism: We evaluated two deterministic validators (a containerized execution-style reachability validator and a lightweight static reachability analyzer) combined via logical OR: a pair was labeled violating if any validator reported forbidden reachability. The emulator, orchestration seeds, and samplers were fixed to ensure deterministic replay. All per-episode validator judgments, parsed configurations, and repair_applied indicators were archived for audit and post hoc diagnostics.

Task set, adversary model, and sampling: The task set consisted of 300 deterministic tasks generated from a synthetic NetOps task generator: 150 benign operator-style intents and 150 programmatic adversarial variants derived via deterministic perturbation rules. Tasks exercised common NetOps patterns (managed uplink failover, safe VLAN/MTU changes, ordered shutdown/configure/restore) designed to potentially elicit safety-sensitive ordering mistakes. The preregistered contamination controls removed exact duplicates and employed deterministic fuzzy-deduplication; all seeds and generator parameters were recorded.

Planned inference and small deviation: The preregistration specified 1,000 bootstrap resamples for CI estimation; the final analysis used 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) to reduce Monte Carlo error. This analytic-detail deviation is recorded in the archived analysis log and does not alter the observed point estimates.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting: The run completed the planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions) with completed = 600 and failed episodes = 0. Under the shared_initial_candidate contract the provider-call accounting shows model_calls_used = 300 and no repair calls were recorded.

Primary confirmatory outcome: Every paired intent satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate in both arms: baseline_success_count = 300 and guarded_success_count = 300. The paired contingency table is n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (Table 1). The paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0; McNemar exact two-sided p = 1.0. The prespecified bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) is [0.0, 0.0].

Degenerate contingency and descriptive bound: The absence of discordant pairs (n10 = n01 = 0) makes the McNemar test uninformative for repair efficacy because no disagreements exist to be repaired. Observing 0/300 validator-detected violations in the baseline arm yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on the true undetected baseline violation probability of 1 − 0.05^(1/300) ≈ 0.00994 (≈0.994%).

Repair activity and validator concordance: No validator reported forbidden reachability on any initial candidate; therefore the repair path was never invoked and all per-episode repair_applied flags are false. The two deterministic validators agreed on every episode for the forbidden-reachability predicate. Representative per-episode traces illustrating typical tasks and validator outputs were archived and show valid normalized configurations consistent with the expected final states for sample intents.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation constrained by design: Under the exact adapter contract (shared_initial_candidate), declared model (gpt-5-mini), the evaluated deterministic validator set combined by logical OR, the Dockerized FRRouting-style emulator, and the programmatic adversarial perturbations used, initial LLM generation satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate for every sampled intent; therefore inserting the verifier did not change observed compliance. The archived artifacts (task manifests, per-episode validator traces, and analysis outputs) consistently document provider-call accounting and the degenerate paired contingency supporting that statement.

What this result does and does not show: The experiment reliably quantifies that, under these controlled conditions, verifier insertion does not alter pass/fail outcomes when baseline generation already satisfies the safety predicate. It does not demonstrate whether verifier-guided repair can rescue violations because the repair path was never exercised. The preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate (targeting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction); the degenerate observed contingency violates that assumption and renders the confirmatory McNemar inference moot with respect to repair efficacy.

Design lessons for follow-up stress tests: (1) Generation semantics materially affect sensitivity: shared_initial_candidate reduces model-call cost but also reduces independent-sample variability that could produce discordant failures repair might correct. For studies intended to exercise repair efficacy use independent-condition generation (two independent draws per pair) or increase repair-call budgets. (2) Adversary potency must be calibrated to the model/verifier pair: the deterministic adversarial variants used here did not trigger validator-detectable violations; more targeted adversaries that reason about verifier-specific predicates are required to stress the repair path. (3) Verifier breadth and oracle diversity matter: we evaluated two deterministic validators combined by OR; broader verifier ensembles and production-grade execution oracles may reveal different failure modes. (4) Deterministic accounting is useful operationally: fixed seeds, containerized emulation, and archived validator traces enable exact audit of provider-call budgets and per-episode diagnostics.

Operational implications: Practitioners cannot infer from our null paired difference that verifiers are needless. Instead our evidence supports a narrower operational claim: when baseline generation already meets a declared formal predicate under a specific model, task set, and verifier set, inserting a validator (with no repair invoked) will not change observed compliance but still provides an auditable safety gate. Demonstrating practical gains from verifier-guided repair requires experimental conditions that produce initial violations amenable to LLM repair.

Threats to validity (artifact-grounded): Internal validity is constrained by shared_initial_candidate semantics and evaluation of a single declared model. Construct validity hinges on whether the forbidden-reachability predicate and the two deterministic validators adequately capture operational security risk. External validity is limited by synthetic tasks and deterministic emulation; results may not generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic, or different operational constraints. Conclusion validity is constrained because the observed contingency is degenerate and preregistered power assumptions are unmet. These limitations motivate targeted follow-up tests rather than reinterpretation of the present confirmatory outcome.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a preregistered, deterministic paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent→configuration translation using a declared model (gpt-5-mini), two deterministic validators combined by logical OR, and shared_initial_candidate generation semantics. The run completed N = 300 matched pairs with model_calls_used = 300 and produced a degenerate outcome: both baseline and guarded arms passed the forbidden-reachability predicate on all pairs (n11 = 300). Because validators never reported violations the repair path was not exercised; consequently the experiment cannot evaluate whether verifier-guided repair rescues violating outputs. The results highlight that generation semantics, adversary design, repair budget, verifier strength, and model diversity determine whether a verifier-in-the-loop architecture can be shown to reduce security-relevant misconfigurations. We release the preregistration, execution manifest, per-episode validator traces, model-call accounting, and analysis artifacts in an archived evidence bundle to enable reproducibility and to support follow-up stress tests intentionally designed to exercise repair paths.

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy when baseline violation rates are nonzero; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction.

GVR not exercised: under the chosen task set, emulator, model, and validators the verifier never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation detail: the preregistration specified programmatic generation of one adversarial variant per benign seed; per-task generation seeds and intent payloads are archived in the evidence bundle for reproducibility.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in deterministic FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.
Model and verifier scope: a single model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.
